title: The Galactic Center above the ESO 3.6-meter telescope
caption: The center of the Milky Way above the ESO 3.6-meter telescope, La Silla Observatory
celestial: Photograph taken at La Silla Observatory, Chile

recognition.text: Published in the ESO image archive. No published rating.

story: The Milky Way stretches across the frame, a disc-shaped galaxy seen perfectly edge-on. Above the dome of the ESO 3.6-meter telescope, lit by the Moon, rises its yellowish central bulge, partly hidden behind dark clouds of dust. Following the dark lane that climbs from the center toward the top leads, according to the source, to the reddish nebula around Antares.

Our galaxy holds hundreds of billions of stars along with plenty of gas and dust. The dust absorbs visible light and re-emits it at longer wavelengths, so to our eyes it looks completely opaque. Ancient Andean civilisations saw animal-shaped constellations in these dark lanes. The Galactic Center lies in Sagittarius and is best seen in the southern winter.
The telescope, inaugurated in 1976, works with the HARPS spectrograph, which ESO calls the world's most precise exoplanet hunter. La Silla was ESO's first site in Chile.

understand.summary: This is a night landscape photograph by Alexandre Santerne. The source gives no camera or color details.
understand.eye: Dust in the Milky Way absorbs visible light and looks opaque to the eye, which is why the lanes appear dark.

explore: La Silla lies 600 km north of Santiago, at 2400 m on the outskirts of the Atacama Desert, and was the largest observatory of its time. ESO Photo Ambassador Alexandre Santerne took the photograph while the telescope was observing.
alt: A telescope dome lit by moonlight beneath the edge-on band of the Milky Way, with a bright yellowish bulge partly hidden by dark dust lanes.
